job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Iris Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my grandmother in a flat above her sewing shop on Mill Lane, and take the bus to Harcourt University for my master's in power systems. Days are lectures on grid protection and long hours in the lab, where I'm testing a relay for my project. In the evenings I help my grandmother with her accounts and cook dinner. I did a bachelor's in electrical engineering, then eight weeks last summer at a regional grid operator, and I owe about 30,000 with nothing saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected. Software has always saved a little time here and there, and nobody has replaced engineers over a spreadsheet. I'd probably say nothing online, because I don't like arguing about things I can't check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a relief, but it doesn't solve much for me. The jobs at the grid operator open once or twice a year, and the local utility took two graduates last year. I'd still be applying against fifty others with a debt that's bigger than a year's pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, and apply for the grid operator's graduate scheme and the three utilities within an hour or two by bus. I'd keep working on my relay project so there's something real to talk about at interviews. And I'd keep cooking and doing the accounts at home, because that's how I pay my way there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, with a weight on my shoulders. Money, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the job you're aiming for, and how many exist nearby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe five suitable posts a year within an hour's journey. Most want a year of experience, and I have eight weeks. I'd get through the first filter on my degree and then hope the internship counts for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your grandmother say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandmother says to study and eat properly, and that everything else sorts itself out. She's been through harder times than a job market. I don't tell her about the debt, because she'd try to give me her shop savings, and I won't take them.

say: I'd say it's what I **expected**: software saves a little time and nobody replaces engineers over a spreadsheet.
I'd stay quiet online, since I don't argue about things I can't check.
think: Privately it's a relief, but the grid operator hires **once or twice** a year.
I'd be one of fifty against a **30,000 debt**.
do: Apply to the **grid operator's graduate scheme** and three utilities within an hour's bus ride.
Keep working on my **relay project** to talk about at interviews.
feel: **Steady** but with a weight on my shoulders, mostly money.
S0.quote: Maybe five suitable posts a year within an hour's journey. Most want a year of experience, and I have eight weeks.
fieldNote: Iris counts the **posts** in her area exactly, which shows her pragmatism.
The AI question barely touches her; her anxiety is local scarcity and debt.
She hides the debt from her grandmother to protect the shop savings.

steps.text: Apply to the grid operator's graduate scheme before its October deadline
Finish the relay protection project and prepare it as an interview talking point

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see. Many things get announced and few arrive, and I'd want to see it in a real company before saying it's happening. If it does, I'd expect everyone to adjust, and I'd rather not panic ahead of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it touches my work more than I let on. A lot of my internship was drawing diagrams, checking calculations and writing reports about network faults. If software does those quickly, they need fewer people for the same jobs, and I'm applying to exactly those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay with the course I know and make sure the hands-on part of my degree is strong, because someone has to climb the pole or test the substation. I'd ask the grid operator if a site-based graduate role exists. I wouldn't start with AI tools, because I haven't needed them, though I might ask a friend to show me one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautious. A little low, if I'm honest, because everything feels harder when positions are already so few.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of grid engineering do you think software takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Diagram drawing, fault calculations and the reports. A supervisor named Mr Takeda spent half his days on those. I could see how software could do most of it by lunchtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it change what you'd study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the electrical side, which is about physical equipment. I'd go for protection and commissioning, where you have to visit a site and sign off. It's less glamorous, but it's where software is slower to reach.

say: I'd say many things get **announced** and few arrive, so I'd rather not panic ahead of time.
I'd want to see it in a real company before believing it.
think: It touches my work more than I let on: **diagrams, checks and reports** were my internship.
They'd need fewer people for the same jobs, and I'm applying for **exactly those**.
do: Ask the grid operator about a **site-based** graduate role.
Focus on **protection and commissioning**, where someone must visit a site and sign off.
feel: **Cautious** and a little low, since positions are already few.
S1.quote: I'd go for protection and commissioning, where you have to visit a site and sign off. It's less glamorous, but it's where software is slower to reach.
fieldNote: Iris's public line is **wait and see**, but privately she maps her internship tasks to what software takes.
She picks site-based electrical work as shelter.
Mr Takeda's half-day spent on reports is her evidence.

steps.text: Apply for site-based commissioning and protection roles at utilities
Wait until an employer I apply to actually adopts the software
Ask a classmate to show me one AI tool for fault reports

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that this one needs the government and the big employers to sit down and plan. Individuals can't solve it. I'd stay calm in public, because panic helps nobody, but I'd say we should know what the plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be very afraid. The jobs I'd apply for are thinking jobs, planning and protection design. If the AI does that in two years, I'd graduate into nothing. The site jobs would last a bit longer, but robots come around 2031 and I'd be in my thirties by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the course, because the loan needs me enrolled and a degree is still a degree. I'd apply for site apprenticeships and anything at the utilities, even a cable-pulling job. I'd move my savings, which is nearly nothing, to the safest account and ask my aunt for her spare room, so I can leave the lane and cut rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Like a long grey afternoon that doesn't end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two years do to your degree plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably stop the idea of a PhD, which I'd half planned. If the thinking work goes first, a PhD is the least useful thing I could do. I'd think about a trade certificate, or an electrician's licence, which pays quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government, first. Then employers who've made profits from the old system, and the universities that sell the degrees. I'm not angry at the machine, I'm angry at the lack of anyone's plan.

say: I'd say governments and big employers must **sit down and plan**, because individuals can't solve this.
I'd stay calm in public, since **panic** helps nobody.
think: The jobs I'd apply for are **thinking jobs**, so I'd graduate into very little.
Site work lasts longer, but **robots** arrive about 2031 and I'd be in my thirties.
do: Finish the master's and apply for **site apprenticeships** and cable-pulling jobs.
Look into an **electrician's licence** that pays quickly.
feel: **Heavy**, like a long grey afternoon that doesn't end.
S2.quote: If the thinking work goes first, a PhD is the least useful thing I could do.
fieldNote: Iris has already **half planned** a PhD and drops it in this world.
Her fear is for the whole path; the trade licence is her practical answer.
She is angry at planners and employers, not at the machine.

steps.text: Look into an electrician's licence course that pays quickly
Apply for site apprenticeships and cable-pulling jobs at the utilities
Ask my aunt about her spare room to cut rent
Move my last 200 into the safest savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for governments to move if they start now. I'd want a plan on what happens to graduates and to people near retirement. I'd keep my views to myself, but I'd vote for people with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years lets me get one real job behind me. If I'm in a protection team by 2027, I'd have some track record by 2031. It's a gamble that the site work lasts, but it's the best one I can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any graduate job in the sector, including a poor one, and keep my evening accounts job for my grandmother's shop as backup. I'd put 100 a month toward the loan. And I'd study for the grid operator's technical exam, since certified people are harder to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. Not scared, but wary, like waiting for weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the electrical field, the site focus, and my relay project. I'd drop the idea of a PhD. I'd probably keep my evening job helping my grandmother with her accounts for as long as she needs me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your plans would you keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also start to learn the software side, grudgingly. If I'm going to check a substation design, I'd better understand what the tools do wrong. That's about the limit of my curiosity.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** for governments to move if they start now.
I'd vote for people with a **plan** for graduates and people near retirement.
think: Five years lets me get **one real job** behind me and some track record by 2031.
The site work lasting is a **gamble**, but the best one I can see.
do: Take **any graduate job** in the sector and put 100 a month toward the loan.
Study for the grid operator's **technical exam**, since certified people are harder to replace.
S3.quote: I'd study for the grid operator's technical exam, since certified people are harder to replace.
fieldNote: Iris answers every scenario with **certified, site-based** work.
Learning AI tools only comes up reluctantly and for checking others' work.
She would keep helping her grandmother with the shop accounts.

steps.text: Take the first graduate job at a utility, even a poor one
Pay 100 a month toward the loan
Study for the grid operator's technical exam in the evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and most things sort themselves out, as they usually do. I'd tell friends to make sure they have a skill someone has to be in the room for. That's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd feel mostly fine. I'd have a decade to get settled, pay the debt and maybe own a flat. I'd have a job, I'd probably be senior in a team, and the AI would change the paperwork more than the substation. The robots come about 2039, but by then I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd graduate, take the first job and stick with it for a few years. I'd pay the loan off by about 32, and save for a deposit with my cousin Wen. I'd learn to use the new tools when my team has to. That's my style, I'm afraid. Slow and steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. A little sleepy, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandmother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't worry, and I'd bring her the first payslip. She'd want to see it printed, not on a screen. She doesn't trust screens, and I find I don't either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would ten years change for a plan like yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade is enough to be late and still catch up. That suits me, because I'm usually the one who's late to new things.

say: I'd say most things **sort themselves out**, and tell friends to hold a skill someone has to be in the room for.
think: I'd feel mostly fine with a decade to **get settled** and pay the debt.
AI would change the **paperwork** more than the substation.
do: Take a **first job** and stay a few years, paying the loan off by about 32.
Save for a **deposit** with my cousin Wen.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The one with two years. It leaves nothing to prepare, and I'd have debt and no experience. What would help is a government plan I can read, an apprenticeship route into the grid sector that pays something, and rules that make companies train juniors instead of dropping them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No. Only that I'm not used to these questions. People usually ask what I'm going to do, not how I feel. It was good to say it out loud.

headlineQuote: People usually ask what I'm going to do, not how I feel. It was good to say it out loud.
portrait: Iris is 24, finishing a **power systems master's** after electrical engineering, with 30,000 of debt and no savings.
She lives with her grandmother above a sewing shop and hides the debt from her, so the shop savings stay untouched.
She is centrist and practical, **never uses AI**, and answers every scenario with site-based, certified electrical work.
She is anxious in most worlds and alarmed at two years, easing to uneasy with a decade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**: no time, debt, and only eight weeks of experience.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a readable **government plan**, a paid grid apprenticeship route and rules that make firms train juniors.
